design_detail: Critical narrative review organized around six a priori hypotheses that would each support a causal effect of methamphetamine on cognition if confirmed: animal dosing studies, well-matched cross-sectional human studies (15 studies in Table 1), a twin study, cognition with abstinence, brain change with abstinence, and dose–response. Written partly in response to Hart et al. (2012).
can_establish: Which lines of indirect evidence exist for a causal effect, how strong each is, and where they fail (notably the absence of dose–response), with checkable citations.
cannot_establish: A quantitative or bias-adjusted estimate: there is no systematic search for most hypotheses, no risk-of-bias assessment and no pooling; the lines of evidence it combines share the same confounds, so their agreement is weaker than independent confirmation.

sample.inclusion_exclusion: Stated only for the cross-sectional hypothesis: diagnosis of methamphetamine dependence (usually SCID), exclusion of comorbid psychiatric and medical conditions and of current dependence on other drugs, urine-verified abstinence at testing, and groups matched or statistically controlled for age, sex, education and estimated IQ (p. 261). No databases, terms or dates are reported for any hypothesis.
sample.selection_effects: Completeness cannot be checked. Several reviewed studies come from the authors' own group (e.g. Simon et al., 2010; Morales et al., 2012; Dean et al., 2012; Monterosso et al., 2005).

exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Estimates human intake in dependent users at 0.5–1.4 g/day, about 6–17.5 mg/kg/day for an 80-kg adult, and 0.60–3.5 mg/kg per dose, to compare with animal regimens; notes rats metabolize methamphetamine faster, so equal mg/kg doses may not be equivalent (p. 260). Reported here as the review's dose-translation reasoning, not as use guidance.
exposure.polysubstance: Notes polysubstance use is extremely common and nicotine dependence was not excluded in most studies (p. 261).

comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Acknowledged as the central limitation of cross-sectional studies (p. 261); argues that matching on education may under-correct because methamphetamine use can cut schooling short (pp. 267–268).

outcomes.operationalization: Treats mild group-level differences as evidence of mild decline in the construct measured, rejecting a categorical normal/impaired reading (p. 270).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Argues Bonferroni correction is over-conservative for intercorrelated cognitive tests (p. 261).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. Vote counts: of 7 well-matched studies, 6 found users worse on some tests; of 8 statistically controlled studies, 5 did (p. 261). Most significant differences were within 1 SD (p. 261). Simon et al. (2010): users improved 0.14 SD more than controls over a month, p=0.33 (p. 264).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Animal studies show cognitive deficits after chronic or binge dosing, partly prevented by prior dose escalation; matched cross-sectional studies mostly show users worse on a subset of tests, usually by less than 1 SD; one twin study shows mixed results; controlled longitudinal studies show no significant group-by-time recovery; brain measures change during early abstinence in small studies; dose–response is mostly absent.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract speaks of the possibility that methamphetamine causes mild decline in some users (p. 259); the discussion states it does cause mild decline in at least some individuals (pp. 268–270). The causal step rests on combining lines of evidence that share confounds (selection, premorbid differences, practice effects) and on weighting animal evidence most heavily (p. 268) despite the dose-translation caveats the review itself raises (p. 260). Support for recovery with abstinence is called mild although both controlled longitudinal studies were null on their primary comparisons (p. 264).

timeline.event: The critical review this paper answers
Meta-analysis of 44 studies: moderate average deficits, strong publication bias
Meta-analysis of abstinent samples: small-to-moderate differences; strong statements premature
Meta-analysis of 68 newer studies: medium-to-large average differences; GRADE very low

replication.where_it_stands: Its framing (mild average decline, present in some users, causality indirect) is close to where later meta-analyses landed on magnitude; the causal question remains open.

funding.funder: NIH grants K23 DA927734, DA 022539, DA 020726, DA 15179, T32 DA024635, F31 DA028812; endowments from the Thomas P and Katherine K Pike Chair in Addiction Studies and the Marjorie M Greene Trust (p. 270).
funding.declared_conflicts: Dr London receives funding from Philip Morris USA for UCLA's Adolescent Smoking Cessation Center; the other authors declare none (p. 270).
funding.affiliations_note: Recorded as declared; not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts with cognitive testing before regular use; and longitudinal abstinence studies with retested controls and individual-level normative impairment rates, pre-registered.

domains.note: No databases, terms or dates for any hypothesis.

domains.domain: Inclusion criteria and list of excluded studies
domains.note: Explicit criteria for the cross-sectional hypothesis only (p. 261).

domains.domain: Risk of bias assessed in included studies

domains.domain: Risk of bias considered when interpreting results

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a systematic summary, critically low (no search, vote counting). As an argument, it is transparent about which hypotheses failed (dose–response) and gives checkable numbers.

key_findings.finding: Chronic or binge dosing produces cognitive deficits in rodents and monkeys; escalating-dose pretreatment prevented binge-induced deficits in several rat studies, while escalating regimens still produced selective deficits in vervet monkeys that improved with abstinence (Groman et al., 2012).

Of 7 well-matched cross-sectional studies, 6 found users worse on some tests (1 small study found none); of 8 statistically controlled studies, 5 did; no matched study found users better on any test; most differences were within 1 SD.
Twin study (Toomey et al., 2003; 50 male pairs, 80% amphetamine): stimulant-using twins worse on 4 of 14 tests and better on 1 (sustained attention); no urinalysis at testing.

Controlled longitudinal abstinence studies: Simon et al. (2010) found no significant extra improvement over a month (0.14 SD, p=0.33); Iudicello et al. (2010) found no significant group change over a year, with a post hoc trend (p=0.06) in a subgroup impaired at baseline, some subgroups as small as 6.
Pre–post studies without retested controls (Volkow et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2004; Jaffe et al., 2005) cannot separate improvement from practice effects.
Brain changes during abstinence (DAT, glucose metabolism, grey matter) come from studies of 5, 5, 10 and 12 users; the grey-matter study used an uncorrected threshold (p<0.001, cluster >100 voxels).
Most studies found no relation between cognition and duration, frequency or estimated lifetime amount of use; positive findings came from post hoc analyses without Type I error control.
Age of first use correlated with years of education (r=−0.48) and with the shortfall of actual versus cognitively predicted education (r=−0.42) in 36 users (Dean et al., 2012).

The authors conclude the preponderance of evidence supports mild cognitive decline in at least some users, with average performance in the low-average to average range, and disagree with treating normed scores categorically.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract frames the causal conclusion as a possibility; the discussion states it as established for at least some individuals.
reporting_issues.consequence: The strength of the causal claim shifts between sections.

reporting_issues.issue: 'No matched study found users better' is offered as evidence against chance findings, but selective publication would produce the same pattern, and the twin study did find one test favouring users.
reporting_issues.consequence: The argument against Type I error is weaker than presented.
